metaTitle: Spain Remote Worker Tax Calculator 2026 | Remotax
metaDescription: Calculate 2026 Spain net pay under standard IRPF and 24% Beckham Law. Compare employee vs autónomo rates, {{es.employee.maxAnnualBaseFormatted}} SS cap, and Madrid living costs.
intro: At €100,000 gross income, a remote employee in Spain retains {{es.netPay100kStdEmployeeFormatted}} net under standard IRPF ({{es.effectiveRate100kStdEmployee}} effective rate), or {{es.netPay100kBeckhamEmployeeFormatted}} net ({{es.effectiveRate100kBeckhamEmployee}} effective rate) under the 24% Beckham Law. Remote contractors take home {{es.netPay100kStdContractorFormatted}} ({{es.effectiveRate100kStdContractor}} effective rate). Employee social security contributions cap at {{es.employee.maxAnnualSSRoundedFormatted}} annually. Self-employed autónomo contributions evaluate the statutory minimum base across 15 income tramos ({{es.autonomo.minCuotaFormatted}} to {{es.autonomo.maxCuotaFormatted}} monthly, totaling {{es.autonomo.maxAnnualSSRoundedFormatted}} annually in our model), while an autónomo electing the maximum contribution base pays up to {{es.autonomo.optionalMaxMonthlyCuotaFormatted}} monthly ({{es.autonomo.optionalMaxAnnualSSFormatted}} annually).
taxSystemOverview: Under the statutory framework of the Impuesto sobre la Renta de las Personas Físicas (IRPF), international professionals residing in Spain for more than {{es.daysResidency}} days in a calendar year are classified as domestic tax residents. Spain assesses progressive personal income tax through a bifurcated statutory structure consisting of a state scale (escala general estatal) and an autonomous community scale (escala autonómica). For fiscal year 2026, standard combined tax brackets range from {{es.taxBrackets.minRatePercent}} on income up to {{es.taxBrackets.minBracketLimit}} to {{es.taxBrackets.maxRatePercent}} on earnings exceeding {{es.taxBrackets.topThresholdFormatted}}. Salaried workers benefit from standard statutory deductions including a {{es.deductions.workExpenseAllowanceFormatted}} general deductible expense allowance and personal exemptions of {{es.deductions.standardAllowanceFormatted}}.
socialSecurityAnalysis: For salaried remote employees, standard social security contributions total {{es.employee.ratePercent}} of gross pay in 2026, comprising common contingencies ({{es.employee.contingencyRatePercent}}), unemployment ({{es.employee.unemploymentRatePercent}}), professional training ({{es.employee.trainingRatePercent}}), and the Mechanism of Intergenerational Equity (MEI) contribution of {{es.employee.meiRatePercent}} under Orden PJC/297/2026. Employee contributions are subject to a statutory maximum contribution base of {{es.employee.maxMonthlyBaseFormatted}} per month ({{es.employee.maxAnnualBaseFormatted}} annually), capping total annual employee contributions at {{es.employee.maxAnnualSSFormatted}}. Conversely, self-employed contractors (autónomos) are subject to the real-income contribution framework enacted by Real Decreto-ley 13/2022. Autónomos deduct a standard {{es.autonomo.expenseProvisionPercent}} generic provision for business expenses, after which net income is mapped across {{es.autonomo.tramoCount}} statutory contribution brackets (tramos). For 2026, monthly autónomo payments using the minimum base range from {{es.autonomo.minCuotaFormatted}} for net returns under {{es.autonomo.minMonthlyNetFormatted}} monthly up to {{es.autonomo.maxCuotaFormatted}} for returns exceeding {{es.autonomo.maxMonthlyNetThresholdFormatted}} monthly, establishing a baseline self-employed annual contribution of {{es.autonomo.maxAnnualSSFormatted}} in our model. Autónomos who choose a higher contribution base up to the statutory maximum of {{es.employee.maxMonthlyBaseFormatted}} monthly pay up to {{es.autonomo.optionalMaxMonthlyCuotaFormatted}} monthly ({{es.autonomo.optionalMaxAnnualSSFormatted}} annually).
specialRegimeSummary: The Spanish Special Expatriate Regime (Beckham Law, Art. 93 LIRPF), expanded under the Startup Act (Ley 28/2022) to encompass international digital nomads and qualified remote employees, allows incoming professionals to be taxed as non-residents on Spanish-source employment income. Under this regime, qualifying individuals are subject to a flat tax rate of {{es.beckham.ratePercent}} on gross earnings up to {{es.beckham.capFormatted}}, with a {{es.beckham.overflowRatePercent}} marginal rate applying strictly to income exceeding that threshold. This regime completely bypasses standard progressive brackets and exempts non-Spanish investment dividends and foreign capital gains from Spanish taxation for the year of relocation plus the subsequent 5 tax years.
costOfLivingAnalysis: In our statutory baseline model, monthly baseline living expenditures in Madrid are estimated at {{es.livingCostFormatted}} for a single professional, encompassing private apartment rental in central neighborhoods, utilities, telecommunications, groceries, and dining. While secondary cities such as Valencia, Seville, or Málaga provide lower rental averages (€1,300 to €1,500 monthly), Madrid and Barcelona offer superior international connectivity, co-working infrastructure, and high-speed rail transit.
whatEstimateExcludes: This calculation models national IRPF statutory scales and the baseline autonomous scale, but does not incorporate regional variance across specific autonomous communities (e.g. Madrid vs Catalonia). It also excludes Spain's Wealth Tax (Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio) and the national Temporary Solidarity Tax on Large Fortunes, which apply only to net global assets exceeding €3,000,000. For contractors, Value Added Tax (IVA at 21%) is excluded, as B2B cross-border professional services to foreign clients are generally subject to reverse-charge zero-rating rules.

faqs.q: What is the primary qualification criteria for Spain's 24% Beckham Law in 2026?
faqs.a: To qualify for the Beckham Law, you must not have been a tax resident in Spain during the 5 tax years preceding your arrival. You must move to Spain under an employment contract with an employer, under an assignment letter, or as a qualifying international digital nomad holding the Spanish Digital Nomad Visa. An application must be submitted to the Agencia Tributaria (Form 149) within 6 months of registering with Spanish Social Security.

faqs.q: How does Spain tax remote contractors versus remote salaried employees in 2026?
faqs.a: Salaried remote employees contribute {{es.employee.ratePercent}} to Social Security capped at {{es.employee.maxAnnualSSRoundedFormatted}} annually and deduct {{es.deductions.workExpenseAllowanceFormatted}} in general employment expenses. Registered self-employed contractors (autónomos) pay monthly social security cuotas based on 15 real-income tramos. Our model uses the statutory minimum base of each tramo (ranging from {{es.autonomo.minCuotaFormatted}} to {{es.autonomo.maxCuotaFormatted}} monthly, or {{es.autonomo.minAnnualSSFormatted}} to {{es.autonomo.maxAnnualSSRoundedFormatted}} annually). An autónomo may choose a higher contribution base up to {{es.employee.maxMonthlyBaseFormatted}} monthly, resulting in cuotas up to {{es.autonomo.optionalMaxMonthlyCuotaFormatted}} monthly ({{es.autonomo.optionalMaxAnnualSSFormatted}} annually). Legitimate business expenses are deductible before applying progressive IRPF rates.

faqs.q: At what gross salary does the Beckham Law become more advantageous than standard IRPF?
faqs.a: Because standard IRPF progressive rates start at {{es.taxBrackets.minRatePercent}} and benefit from personal allowances and employment deductions, standard progressive taxation results in lower effective tax below approximately €52,000 to €55,000 for single employees. Above {{es.beckham.advantageThresholdFormatted}} gross salary, the {{es.beckham.ratePercent}} flat rate provides substantial savings, expanding rapidly at €100,000 and higher earnings levels.

faqs.q: Does Spain tax my worldwide income if I spend more than 183 days in the country?
faqs.a: Yes. If you spend more than {{es.daysResidency}} days in Spain during a calendar year without Beckham Law election, you become a standard Spanish tax resident liable to Spanish progressive IRPF on your worldwide income, including offshore dividends, capital gains, and remote overseas business income. Electing the Beckham Law limits taxation primarily to Spanish-source employment earnings.

faqs.q: Are foreign remote contractors eligible for the Beckham Law in Spain?
faqs.a: Under the Startup Act reforms, foreign digital nomads who operate as independent contractors can qualify for the Beckham Law if they hold the formal Spanish Digital Nomad Visa, provided that no more than {{es.beckham.foreignInvoicingLimitPercent}} of their total professional turnover is billed to entities established inside Spain.
